lesson.title: Three Paths to Power: How England's Colonies Governed Themselves
lesson.summary: English colonies in America developed along three main governmental models, royal, proprietary, and charter, each shaping how power was distributed between crown appointed officials and locally elected assemblies across the colonial regions.
lesson.body:
By the late seventeenth century, England's American colonies had settled into three broad patterns of government, each reflecting different origins and different relationships to the crown. Royal colonies were governed directly by the English monarch, who appointed a governor to enforce royal policy and oversee colonial affairs, a structure that eventually applied to Virginia after 1624, when the crown revoked the Virginia Company's charter following years of disastrous mismanagement and disease, and later to other colonies as well. Proprietary colonies were granted by the crown to an individual or small group of proprietors who held broad authority to establish laws and government, subject to the crown's ultimate oversight, as in Maryland, granted to the Calvert family in 1632, and Pennsylvania, granted to William Penn in 1681. Charter colonies, including Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts Bay in its earliest decades, operated under a charter that gave colonists themselves substantial self governing authority, electing their own governors and legislators with comparatively little day to day interference from England.

Despite these differences, most colonies converged on a broadly similar internal structure: a governor, whether appointed or elected, paired with a bicameral legislature consisting of an upper council, often appointed and drawn from wealthy or well connected colonists, and a lower assembly elected by property owning male colonists. Virginia's House of Burgesses, established in 1619, was the first elected representative assembly in English America and became a model that other colonies followed in establishing their own assemblies, even as the underlying labor and land systems, including the headright system and, later, slavery, shaped who held the property required to vote or hold office.

Colonial governance also varied meaningfully by region in ways connected to each region's distinct economy and culture. In the New England Colonies, the Puritan tradition of self governing congregations translated into a political culture that valued local participation, most visibly expressed in town meetings, alongside colony wide assemblies. In the Middle Colonies, greater religious and ethnic diversity, stemming partly from Dutch origins in New York and Quaker toleration in Pennsylvania, produced governments that had to accommodate a wider range of interests and beliefs than the more religiously uniform New England colonies. In the Southern Colonies, where the plantation economy built on headrights, indentured servitude, and increasingly enslaved labor concentrated wealth and land in relatively few hands, government tended to operate through county courts dominated by local planter elites, who also controlled colony wide assemblies like the House of Burgesses.

These regional patterns of governance were not simply administrative details but reflected the deeper economic and social structures that had developed across the colonies. The concentration of political power among Southern planters, the participatory culture of New England towns, and the negotiated diversity of the Middle Colonies all grew out of the same forces, land, labor, religion, and trade, that had shaped colonial society since the earliest settlements, and these differences would continue to influence American political life well beyond the colonial period.
